Some sounds have been reused so often that you have heard them in songs decades apart without knowing it. The YouTube channel
Synthet goes through seven of them in [*the best samples in history*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0). This page follows
the video: what each sound is, where it came from, and the songs the video plays it in. Every ▶ opens the video at that moment.
All the songs are also in the [Tune Directory](../practice/tune-directory.qmd) (Concepts column, source Synthet).

Why do these sounds spread? The video's answer is the same each time: they are **clean** (drums or one instrument with little else
playing, so a producer can lift them out), **simple** (a groove you can loop for minutes) and played **with feel** by a great player.
Producers then found them on compilations such as *Ultimate Breaks & Beats*, made for exactly this use.

## 1. The Funky Drummer break (2,000+ songs)

James Brown's *Funky Drummer* (1970) has a drum break about five minutes in, played by **Clyde Stubblefield**. The record was no big
hit. By 1986 Brown saw how much hip-hop producers sampled, and re-released the break with the drums alone, *to be sampled*. It worked.

The groove itself is plain: kick and snare, a few quiet **ghost notes** (grace notes) on the snare, and hi-hats. What makes it is the
way it is played. Stubblefield was paid nothing for any of the 2,000 songs: royalties go to songwriters, and the song was credited to
Brown.

|---|---|---|---|
| Funky Drummer | James Brown | 1970 | [▶ 0:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=22s) |
| Rebel Without a Pause | Public Enemy | 1988 | [▶ 1:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=78s) |
| Fuck Tha Police | N.W.A | 1988 | [▶ 1:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=81s) |

The video also plays a Sinéad O'Connor song here, without naming it.

## 2. Apache: a melody and a bongo break (800+ songs)

Jerry Lordan wrote the *Apache* tune and played it to **the Shadows**, whose instrumental was a UK number one in 1960. Their version
is hardly sampled. In 1973 the **Incredible Bongo Band** covered it, starting with a long **bongo break** before the melody; that
version took years to catch on, then spread from hip-hop to everywhere. The Sugarhill Gang's *Apache (Jump On It)* is not a sample:
it copies the Bongo Band's intro and way of playing the tune, and made the melody famous (it was on *The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air*).

| You Can't Dance | LL Cool J | 1985 | [▶ 3:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=228s) |
| That's My Bitch | Jay-Z & Kanye West | 2011 | [▶ 3:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=233s) |
| Sweet Thing | Mick Jagger | 1993 | [▶ 3:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=238s) |

## 3. The Good Times bassline (100+ songs)

The Sugarhill Gang's *Rapper's Delight* (1979) runs on a bassline that is not theirs: it is replayed from **Chic**'s disco hit *Good
Times* from the same year. House producers and Will Smith used it since, and it inspired Queen's *Another One Bites the Dust* (a new
line in the same spirit, not a sample).

| Song | Artist | Year | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rapper's Delight | The Sugarhill Gang | 1979 | [▶ 4:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=290s) |
| What's That Sound | The Beatangers | 2014 | [▶ 4:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=298s) |
| Another One Bites the Dust, inspired by | Queen | 1980 | [▶ 5:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=306s) |
| Good Times | Chic | 1979 | [▶ 5:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=316s) |

## 4. Chic again: Soup for One

Chic, with **Nile Rodgers** on guitar, are among the most sampled bands of all. The video's example: take a short piece of *Soup for
One* (1982), loop it, put a filter on it and change its pitch, and you have Modjo's *Lady* ([Sampling 3](sampling-pitch.qmd) does
the same to a loop on this site).

| Song | Artist | Year | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Soup for One | Chic | 1982 | [▶ 5:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=320s) * |
| Lady (Hear Me Tonight) | Modjo | 2000 | [▶ 5:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=336s) |

## 5. The Think break, "Yeah! Woo!" (4,000+ songs)

Lyn Collins's *Think (About It)* (1972) was produced by James Brown, who put several drum breaks in it with shouted vocal shots over
them. The drummer is **John "Jabo" Starks**, a friend of Clyde Stubblefield's (they stayed friends until they died), and like him
probably never paid for it. The break was on *Ultimate Breaks & Beats* and went into hip-hop first; sped up, it is a staple of drum
and bass and breakbeat, often with the "Yeah! Woo!" pitched up.

## 6. A piano loop: C.R.E.A.M. (400+ songs)

The whole piano of Wu-Tang Clan's *C.R.E.A.M.* (1994) is a sample of the Charmels' *As Long as I've Got You* (1967). Then
*C.R.E.A.M.* became a source itself, mostly **interpolated**: other artists re-sing or replay "Cash rules everything around me"
rather than sampling the record.

| Song | Artist | Year | |
|---|---|---|---|
| As Long as I've Got You | The Charmels | 1967 | [▶ 7:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=445s) * |
| C.R.E.A.M. | Wu-Tang Clan | 1994 | [▶ 7:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=458s) |

## 7. A one-shot: "Champ!" (800+ songs)

The Mohawks' *The Champ* (1968) opens with a shout of "Champ!" (it is hard to make out, which helps) and an organ stab. It was a
dance-floor record for DJs in the 1980s, and from there a sample. It is a **one-shot**: dropped in once, often with an echo so it blends
in, the producer's version of the stock scream in films.

| Song | Artist | Year | |
|---|---|---|---|
| The Champ | The Mohawks | 1968 | [▶ 8:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=492s) * |

| Here Comes the Hotstepper | Ini Kamoze | 1994 | [▶ 9:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=545s) |
| Let's Ride | Q-Tip (of A Tribe Called Quest) | 1999 | [▶ 9:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=553s) |
| You Don't Know Me | Ariana Grande | 2014 | [▶ 9:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K71XefOlJh0&t=560s) |

## Things to try

- Find one of these sounds by ear: play two songs from one table and say where the sample comes in, and whether it was sped up.
- Which of the seven are **breaks**, which **loops**, which a **one-shot**, and which a **replayed** part, not a sample at all
  ([Sampling 1](sampling-what.qmd))?
- Two drummers, thousands of songs, no royalties: why? [Sampling 6](sampling-law.qmd) explains the two copyrights in a record.

*How this page was made:* the song names and years come from the captions the video shows on screen; names marked * have no caption
and come from the narration, so check them before relying on them. Two caption years were corrected from the records' release
years (the Shadows' *Apache*, 1960; *Apache (Jump On It)*, 1981), and Rick Astley's year was added. Times are to the second.
